newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan hopes for early peace talks with India.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan hopes for early peace talks with India.

text.p: Pakistan said on Saturday it hoped for an early resumption of stalled peace talks with arch-rival India and was willing to discuss a troop pullout from a disputed Himalayan glacier.
In New Delhi, a government official said Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral was expected to write to his Pakistani counterpart proposing the two countries resume talks.

The optimistic tone from a Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman, in a briefing to reporters in Islamabad, appeared aimed at playing down Pakistani concern over a 21 percent increase in India's defence budget annouced on Friday.
However the spokesman did say any move that could increase regional insecurity and military confrontation would not be a positive development.

He said Pakistan wanted peaceful negotiated settlement of problems and "honestly believes in normal good-neighbourly relations" between the two countries, which have fought three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947.

He described as "very positive" a letter new Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif had sent to his Indian counterpart H.D. Deve Gowda on Thursday proposing a resumption of official-level talks this month before the two leaders meet to discuss the disputed the Himalayan region of Kashmir and other problems.
"We hope that the response from India will be positive and it will be possible to resume these negotiations at an early date," the spokesman said.
Sharif's letter responded to one Deve Gowda had sent to congratulate the Pakistani prime minister on taking office after his party's landslide victory in February 3 elections.

Deve Gowda told Sharif he wanted talks on a wide range of issues and did not exclude Kashmir, where India is fighting a separatist Moslem revolt in two-thirds of the region it rules. Pakistan controls the rest.
The Pakistani spokesman said Islamabad would give "utmost and serious consideration" if it received a formal proposal for troop withdrawal from the disputed Siachen glacier in Kashmir.

He was commenting on a reported proposal by a senior U.S. official that India and Pakistan first tackle the problem of Siachen, which lies near the Chinese border at the northern end of the Line of Control, or ceasefire line, dividing Kashmir.
The spokesman said India and Pakistan had agreed in 1989 to withdraw their troops from Siachen to positions held in 1972, when a control line was agreed after their 1971 war over Bangladesh.

"However, due to reasons that we are not aware of, India later decided that this agreement could not be implemented," he said. "We are always willing to discuss the question of withdrawal of troops from Siachen provided it is based on agreements and agreed principles."
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robin Raphel suggested at a seminar in Washington on Wednesday that Kashmir could be placed on the agenda of India-Pakistan talks, but not necessarily at the top.

"It may be that India and Pakistan can get together and come up with some kind of negotiating process whereby the political status of Kashmir is not first on the agenda, but rather Siachen is first and trade is second," Raphel was quoted as saying.

For more than a decade, Pakistani and Indian troops have been locked in a confrontation on the icy peaks of the 20,000-foot (6,100-metre) high Siachen, the world's highest battlefield where more people have been killed by harsh weather than by fighting.
